title: ‘It’s a biohazard’: Native communities in US south-west try to recover after flooding intensified by El Niño
text:
On the night of 23 October, Jimmie Goodman was trying to get some rest when his sister, who was recovering from back surgery and having trouble sleeping, woke him. Authorities in their home town of Shiprock, New Mexico, had warned that the nearby San Juan River was at risk of flooding as unprecedented rain fell across the Four Corners region of the south-west US – and so Goodman peeked outside.
“That surge shot directly at us,” said Goodman, 67, describing how the river takes a sharp 90-degree turn near his and his sister’s house in one of the Navajo housing authority’s residential neighborhoods. It just missed the house by about 50ft, he said.
As water from the river began filling their driveway, Goodman, who is Navajo/Diné, went back inside to help his sister into his green Ford pickup. The brother and sister had already loaded the truck with some essentials, but Goodman ran back inside to turn off the main power to the house and save his Taylor Swift CDs before he heard his sister call: “Let’s go!”
When he stepped back outside, Goodman’s foot sank into what he guessed was 6-8in of water. “It was like the Bellagio Casino,” he said.
After a painfully dry year that saw New Mexico record its hottest summer on record, heavy thunderstorms and rains intensified by this year’s El Niño lashed the south-west. In the Four Corners region, two weekend storms in late October and early November caused once-in-a-generation flooding in the flash-flood-prone desert. The San Juan River crested at 21ft near Shiprock, the highest it had been reported there since 1935, and reached levels not seen across much of the region since 1911. As families were ordered to evacuate, the flood waters damaged several wastewater treatment facilities in New Mexico and Utah, causing sewage to flood into the river.
“The San Juan River is a hazmat situation,” Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan county, said in late October. “Do not go in the water.”
Communities across the Four Corners region – where the 27,000 sq mile (70,000 sq km) Navajo Nation reservation stretches across parts of New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – were affected by the rains and ensuing floods. In Dennehotso, Arizona, emergency personnel rescued elders as old as 102 by raft and helicopter. Across the border near Bluff, Utah, residents were ordered to evacuate, and remained hesitant to return weeks later as E coli levels in the river and surrounding soil measured 25 times the norm. And in Rock Point, Arizona, voters decided whether to navigate hazardous muddy roads to reach the polls on election day.
In Shiprock, Goodman and his sister found temporary housing in another one of the Navajo housing authority’s residential neighborhoods – while nearby farmers mourned their flooded fields.
One of the few portions of the Navajo Nation with river access, the Shiprock area is home to many farms that fiber artist and shepherd Kevin Aspaas said grow produce for “all of the communities around the Navajo Nation who don’t have access to this river, who don’t have access to irrigation”. Many of those crops are “traditional to our communities, and are used in ceremonies”, he said.
Aspaas, who himself farms beans, melons, squash and corn about a mile from the river, harvested the last of his beans early after he saw the river flood within a few hundred yards of his crops.
“For the most part it was just worrying about getting everything off of the field,” Aspaas said, speaking during a break from shelling Hopi, Zuni gold and other beans in his uncle’s hogan, a traditional Navajo hut. Some of his friends weren’t as lucky. One saw his entire crop of corn – which was drying after being steamed underground – soaked in flood water. Another family, which has relocated some of their farm equipment to the field where Aspaas’s sheep graze, saw their entire farm and home submerged. With the sewage leakage, that means “they can’t go back into their home”, he said.
“It’s really a biohazard at this point,” Aspaas said, noting community fears not just about the sewage but also “about what kind of chemicals they’re using to treat the human waste”.
Zachariah Ben of Bidii Baby Foods, which operates one farm plot in Shiprock and another off the reservation, echoed those concerns. E coli and treatment chemicals “are leaching into the soil and will be causing significant problems for future growing seasons”, he said in a text message.
But another concern he added is insurance. “Crop insurance doesn’t work the same on tribal trust land” and will “leave Navajo farmers with huge crop and infrastructure losses”, he said.
Ben and his family are now looking at a $100,000 loss after their farm plot, greenhouse and yurt – and their many possessions inside the structures – were all submerged in the flood waters.
It’s not only farmers who are navigating the absence of insurance coverage in the wake of the flooding. Virginia Kirk, who owns a rental company and event space which has served as the central hub for donations in Shiprock, says many displaced families are confused about next steps and looking to each other for support.
After the first wave of flooding, Shiprock experienced large power outages. “People had no electricity. It was getting cold. They couldn’t cook their food,” said Kirk, who owns the Kirk Center in Shiprock.
That’s when Denisa Livingston, who leads the Diné Community Advocacy Alliance, and Mackee Bancroft, a chef who is Ute Mountain Ute and Diné, began bringing in hot meals.
“We are not just people who stepped into the flood response; we are stewards of practicing our ancestral ways of organizing,” Livingston said. She adds that her organizing work, which has included Covid relief and advocating for the Navajo Nation’s first-in-the-nation junk food tax, follows in the footsteps of her uncle Phil Harrison, who advocated for federal compensation for families of uranium miners like her grandfather. She notes that Kirk, whose grandfather was one of the first chief justices of the Navajo Nation’s supreme court, fits into a similar legacy.
After the flooding, the Kirk Center, a leasing and rental company with a large event space called the MOD, was quickly transformed into the central distribution and donation site. “We’re not any organization, we just have space,” Kirk said, speaking between directing community members looking to drop off clothing donations and pick up supplies of sanitary products.
The event space filled up with donations from community members – including pet food, diapers and bottles of water – while outside volunteers distributed coal, hay and wood. With the support of the local groups Turquoise Paws and Soul Dog Rescue, Kirk transformed one of her nearby rental properties into a temporary dog shelter.
Volunteers with the Kirk Center, the Diné Community Advocacy Alliance and the Red Cross have been distributing meals to evacuees – such as Goodman and his sister.
Although they were grateful to find temporary housing, Goodman and his sister had to start fully from scratch – including with a place to sleep. His nephew’s boss bought the brother and sister air mattresses, which Goodman was glad to note had built-in pumps: metal in his elbow and hip from prior surgeries, and his sister’s neuropathy – a nervous system disease not uncommon among children of uranium miners – would prevent them from inflating the mattresses manually.
The floodwaters have begun to recede at their house but the road to their home remains unpassable. Goodman’s been able to make it back a few times on foot to feed his chickens.
The brother and sister are guaranteed housing until 20 November, but then they will need to put down a deposit to stay in the temporary home for another 60 days. “It’s hard to rebuild when you have to pay,” Goodman said, cradling his miniature pinscher, Molly. He hopes the road to his home is soon safe to drive on, and friends will be able to help him and his sister start the long work of rebuilding.
